VIDEO.title: The Hidden Message in Jesus Family Tree REVEALED | Ep. 1 (Matthew 1)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 1 aloud, then walks through what he noticed: a genealogy running from Abraham through David and the kings down to Joseph (vv. 1-17), arranged as three sets of fourteen generations, followed by the account of Joseph and Mary (vv. 18-25).

He calls the genealogy 'more like a symbolic sketch' than an exhaustive list, and asks what would have struck the first hearers, early believers who were probably Jewish and heard the Gospel read aloud, as unusual.

The unusual detail is that Matthew names women: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba ('the wife of Uriah') and Mary, when genealogies normally listed men. He links this to Joseph's plan to divorce Mary quietly, a detail he notes only Matthew records, and concludes that Mary, pregnant before the marriage was completed, would have been seen as a social outcast.

His big idea: God is with the outcast. He tests it against Deuteronomy 10:17-19, Psalm 146:9 and Isaiah 61 (the passage Jesus read in Luke 4). God cares for the sojourner, the orphan and the widow, and His people must as well. He stresses this is about Christians serving the Lord, not about politics or government.
QUOTES: Here's the lesson for the original audience: God is with the outcast.
Since God is tremendously concerned with the outcasts, his people must be as well.
You should be looking for things that are out of the norm... because that means something. That's a call out to pay attention.
Matthew 1 is ultimately a reminder of God's heart.

BACKGROUND.p: The LSB footnote on 1:18 calls betrothal 'the first stage of marriage... more legal than an engagement.' That is why Joseph is already called 'her husband' (1:19) and why ending it meant sending her away, which the LSB notes can be rendered 'divorce'. The LSB cross-references Deuteronomy 22:20-24 and 24:1-4 for the Law's background.

Comparing 1 Chronicles 3:11-12, Matthew moves from Joram straight to Uzziah (also called Azariah), passing over Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah. This fits the video's point that the genealogy is not meant to be exhaustive.

Early church writers such as Irenaeus (late 2nd century) linked Matthew's Gospel with the Hebrews. Modern scholars broadly agree it has a strongly Jewish-Christian orientation, which matches the video's picture of Jewish believers hearing it read aloud.

Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus read Isaiah 61:1-2a and stop at 'the favorable year of the Lord.' The video goes on to read Isaiah 61 through verse 5 ('strangers... foreigners') from Isaiah itself. Those later lines are part of Isaiah's passage, not part of what Luke records Jesus reading aloud.

DEBATES.p: The video's answer: they were outcasts, as Mary would be. Other common proposals: Gentile connections (Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabite, Bathsheba through Uriah the Hittite, possibly Tamar) pointing ahead to the nations; unusual unions through which God worked, preparing readers for Mary; and a display of grace to sinners. The views can overlap.

DEBATES.h: Jonathan Pageau: a gathering of scattered branches
DEBATES.p: From Pageau's newsletter 'Don't take biblical genealogy for granted' (Nov 7, 2026), his interpretation, not Scripture's own words: the genealogy gathers back branches that split off through sin. Scripture: Lot's daughters bore Moab and Ben-ammi, fathers of the Moabites and Ammonites (Genesis 19:30-38); Moabites and Ammonites were barred from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3); yet Ruth the Moabite married Boaz and became David's great-grandmother (Ruth 4:13-17). Pageau reads this as Lot's line being woven back into the line of Christ, and sets it against humanity's scattering (Eden, Cain and Abel, Babel in Genesis 11:1-9) and the promise that all families of the earth will be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3). His point: Jesus is not Messiah because of a spotless lineage; as Messiah He takes in those who went astray, starting with His own family. This does not excuse the sins; it shows a way back through humility, like Ruth, Tamar and Rahab.

Matthew himself counts 3 x 14 (1:17). A widely proposed reason is that the Hebrew letters of David's name (D-W-D) add up to 14. Others see a simple memory structure. The third group also lists 13 names unless Jeconiah is counted twice, and interpreters solve that differently.

Luke 3:23-38 runs from Jesus back to Adam and differs from Matthew between David and Joseph. Proposed harmonizations include Matthew giving Joseph's royal or legal line and Luke Mary's line, or levirate and adoption links. Orthodox interpreters hold both are true; how they fit is debated.

Established: the Greek Septuagint translates Isaiah's ʿalmah with parthenos (virgin), and Matthew quotes it that way. Historic Christian teaching affirms the virginal conception, which Matthew states directly (1:18, 20, 25) and Luke confirms (1:34-35). Debated: the full range of ʿalmah and how Isaiah's sign related to Ahaz's own day.

QUESTIONS: Matthew names Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and 'the wife of Uriah.' Read Genesis 38, Joshua 2, Ruth 1 and 2 Samuel 11. What do their stories show about the kind of people God works through?

Pageau sees Ruth bringing Lot's estranged descendants back into the line of Christ (Genesis 19:36-38; Ruth 4:13-17). What broken branch in your own family history might God still gather in through humility?
Joseph was 'a righteous man' and also 'not wanting to disgrace her' (1:19). How do righteousness and mercy fit together in his response?
The video urges us to look for things that are 'not typical' to the first hearers. What else in Matthew 1 surprises you, and why might Matthew have included it?
Deuteronomy 10:19 grounds love for the sojourner in Israel's own past: 'you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.' How does remembering what God rescued you from shape the way you treat outsiders?
Who is overlooked or pushed to the edge in your own circles of influence? What is one concrete step you could take toward them this week?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The video's lesson for the original audience: since God is tremendously concerned with the outcasts, His people must be as well. The teacher asks each viewer to wrestle with that same lesson as it applies to their own life today, and to decide what to do about it in their own circles of influence.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): Matthew 1:21 says the child is named Jesus because He will save His people from their sins. The outsiders in His family tree point to a Savior who brings sinners in. Welcoming the overlooked is the fruit of having been welcomed by Him, not a way of earning it.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]

That is why Joseph is already called 'her husband' (1:19) and why ending it meant sending her away, which the LSB notes can be rendered 'divorce'. The LSB cross-references Deuteronomy 22:20-24 and 24:1-4 for the Law's background.
- Matthew's list is selective: Comparing 1 Chronicles 3:11-12, Matthew moves from Joram straight to Uzziah (also called Azariah), passing over Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah. This fits the video's point that the genealogy is not meant to be exhaustive.
- Who Matthew wrote for: Early church writers such as Irenaeus (late 2nd century) linked Matthew's Gospel with the Hebrews. Modern scholars broadly agree it has a strongly Jewish-Christian orientation, which matches the video's picture of Jewish believers hearing it read aloud.
- What Luke records Jesus reading: Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus read Isaiah 61:1-2a and stop at 'the favorable year of the Lord.' The video goes on to read Isaiah 61 through verse 5 ('strangers... foreigners') from Isaiah itself. Those later lines are part of Isaiah's passage, not part of what Luke records Jesus reading aloud.

- Jonathan Pageau: a gathering of scattered branches: From Pageau's newsletter 'Don't take biblical genealogy for granted' (Nov 7, 2026), his interpretation, not Scripture's own words: the genealogy gathers back branches that split off through sin. Scripture: Lot's daughters bore Moab and Ben-ammi, fathers of the Moabites and Ammonites (Genesis 19:30-38); Moabites and Ammonites were barred from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3); yet Ruth the Moabite married Boaz and became David's great-grandmother (Ruth 4:13-17). His point: Jesus is not Messiah because of a spotless lineage; as Messiah He takes in those who went astray, starting with His own family. This does not excuse the sins; it shows a way back through humility, like Ruth, Tamar and Rahab.
- Why fourteen?: Matthew himself counts 3 x 14 (1:17). A widely proposed reason is that the Hebrew letters of David's name (D-W-D) add up to 14. Others see a simple memory structure. The third group also lists 13 names unless Jeconiah is counted twice, and interpreters solve that differently.

- Deuteronomy 23:3; Ruth 4:13-17: A Moabite barred, yet Ruth enters David's line (Pageau, Nov 7) (added) https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Deuteronomy23

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Matthew names Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and 'the wife of Uriah.' Read Genesis 38, Joshua 2, Ruth 1 and 2 Samuel 11. What do their stories show about the kind of people God works through?
2. Pageau sees Ruth bringing Lot's estranged descendants back into the line of Christ (Genesis 19:36-38; Ruth 4:13-17). What broken branch in your own family history might God still gather in through humility?
3. Joseph was 'a righteous man' and also 'not wanting to disgrace her' (1:19). How do righteousness and mercy fit together in his response?
4. The video urges us to look for things that are 'not typical' to the first hearers. What else in Matthew 1 surprises you, and why might Matthew have included it?
5. Deuteronomy 10:19 grounds love for the sojourner in Israel's own past: 'you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.' How does remembering what God rescued you from shape the way you treat outsiders?
6. Who is overlooked or pushed to the edge in your own circles of influence? What is one concrete step you could take toward them this week?

## Application
The video's lesson for the original audience: since God is tremendously concerned with the outcasts, His people must be as well. The teacher asks each viewer to wrestle with that same lesson as it applies to their own life today, and to decide what to do about it in their own circles of influence.

Study note (added): Matthew 1:21 says the child is named Jesus because He will save His people from their sins. The outsiders in His family tree point to a Savior who brings sinners in. Welcoming the overlooked is the fruit of having been welcomed by Him, not a way of earning it.
